sentences.zh: 于時清談之士庾龢、韓伯、袁宏等，並相知友。

translations.literal: Among the pure-conversation scholars of the time—Yu He, Han Bo, Yuan Hong, and others—he was all on friendly terms.
translations.idiomatic: He befriended the leading qingtan figures of the day—Yu He, Han Bo, Yuan Hong, and their circle.

sentences.zh: 為秘書郎，累居顯職，終於黃門侍郎。

translations.literal: He served as palace secretary, repeatedly held eminent posts, and ended as gentleman attendant at the yellow gates.
translations.idiomatic: He rose from palace secretary through prominent offices to gentleman attendant at the yellow gates.

sentences.zh: 父子並有文筆傳於世。

translations.literal: Father and son alike left writings that circulated in the world.
translations.idiomatic: Father and son both left writings that circulated widely.

sentences.zh: 劉惔

translations.literal: Liu Tan.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Tan

sentences.zh: 劉惔，字真長，沛國相人也。

translations.literal: Liu Tan, style name Zhenchang, was a native of Xiang in the Principality of Pei.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Tan, courtesy name Zhenchang, came from Xiang in the state of Pei.

sentences.zh: 祖宏，字終嘏，光祿勳。

translations.literal: His grandfather Hong, style name Zhonggu, was superintendent of the imperial household.
translations.idiomatic: His grandfather Liu Hong, courtesy name Zhonggu, served as superintendent of the imperial household.

sentences.zh: 宏兄粹，字純嘏，侍中。

translations.literal: Hong's elder brother Cui, style name Chungu, was palace attendant.
translations.idiomatic: Hong's elder brother Liu Cui, courtesy name Chungu, was a palace attendant.

sentences.zh: 宏弟潢，字沖嘏，吏部尚書。

translations.literal: Hong's younger brother Huang, style name Chonggu, was minister of the ministry of personnel.
translations.idiomatic: Hong's younger brother Liu Huang, courtesy name Chonggu, headed the ministry of personnel.

sentences.zh: 並有名中朝。

translations.literal: All were renowned at court.
translations.idiomatic: All three were celebrated figures at the Jin court.

sentences.zh: 時人語曰：「洛中雅雅有三嘏。

translations.literal: People of the time said: 'In Luoyang, gracefully refined, there are three Gu.'
translations.idiomatic: A contemporary rhyme ran: 'In Luoyang the refined trio bear the name Gu.'

sentences.zh: 」父耽，晉陵太守，亦知名。

translations.literal: His father Dan was governor of Jinling and also well known.
translations.idiomatic: His father Liu Dan governed Jinling and was likewise eminent.

sentences.zh: 惔少清遠，有標奇，與母任氏寓居京口，家貧，織芒屩以為養，雖蓽門陋巷，晏如也。

translations.literal: In youth Tan was clear and remote, marked by distinction; he lodged with his mother Lady Ren at Jingkou. The family was poor and wove straw sandals for their upkeep; though they lived behind a wicker gate in a mean lane, he was perfectly content.
translations.idiomatic: Tan was aloof and luminous even young; he lived with his mother Lady Ren at Jingkou. They were poor and lived by weaving straw sandals; wicker gate and shabby lane left him untroubled.

sentences.zh: 人未之識，惟王導深器之。

translations.literal: Others did not recognize his worth; only Wang Dao deeply esteemed him.
translations.idiomatic: Few saw his quality—only Wang Dao grasped how exceptional he was.

sentences.zh: 後稍知名，論者比之袁羊。

translations.literal: Later he gradually became known; commentators compared him to Yuan Yang.
translations.idiomatic: As his name spread, critics likened him to Yuan Yang.

sentences.zh: 惔喜，還告其母。

translations.literal: Tan was pleased and went home to tell his mother.
translations.idiomatic: Delighted, Tan hurried home to tell his mother.

sentences.zh: 其母，聰明婦人也，謂之曰：「此非汝比，勿受之。

translations.literal: His mother, a clever woman, said to him: 'That is no peer for you—do not accept the comparison.'
translations.idiomatic: She was shrewd: 'That man is beneath you—do not welcome the comparison.'

sentences.zh: 」又有方之范汪者。

translations.literal: Again someone compared him to Fan Wang.
translations.idiomatic: Soon someone ranked him beside Fan Wang.

sentences.zh: 惔復喜，母又不聽。

translations.literal: Tan was pleased again; his mother again forbade it.
translations.idiomatic: Tan glowed again; again she forbade it.

sentences.zh: 及惔年德轉升，論者遂比之荀粲。

translations.literal: When Tan's years and virtue had risen, commentators finally compared him to Xun Can.
translations.idiomatic: Only when Tan had matured in age and reputation did critics dare compare him to Xun Can.

sentences.zh: 尚明帝女廬陵公主。

translations.literal: He married the Princess of Luling, daughter of Emperor Ming.
translations.idiomatic: He married Emperor Ming's daughter, the Princess of Luling.

sentences.zh: 以惔雅善言理，簡文帝初作相，與王濛並為談客，俱蒙上賓禮。

translations.literal: Because Tan excelled at reasoning in conversation, when Emperor Jianwen first served as chief minister he and Wang Meng were both retained as discourse guests and alike received the honors due foremost guests.
translations.idiomatic: Tan probed principle in conversation so keenly that when the future Emperor Jianwen first headed the secretariat, he and Wang Meng became his salon regulars and received the honors reserved for chief guests.

sentences.zh: 時孫盛作《易象妙於見形論》，帝使殷浩難之，不能屈。

translations.literal: At the time Sun Sheng had composed 'On the Wonder of the Images of the Changes Surpassing Visible Form'; the emperor had Yin Hao challenge it but could not refute it.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Sheng had written "On the Wonder of the Images of the Changes Surpassing Visible Form"; the prince assigned Yin Hao to debate it, yet Yin could not break it.

sentences.zh: 帝曰：「使真長來，故應有以制之。

translations.literal: The emperor said: 'If Zhenchang came, there ought to be something to master it.'
translations.idiomatic: He said, 'Let Zhenchang take the floor—he will find a way to corner it.'

sentences.zh: 」乃命迎惔。

translations.literal: He then ordered Tan to be summoned.
translations.idiomatic: He sent for Liu Tan.

sentences.zh: 盛素敬服惔，及至，便與抗答，辭甚簡至，盛理遂屈。

translations.literal: Sheng had always respected Tan; when Tan arrived he debated him directly, his wording very concise, and Sheng's reasoning was defeated.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Sheng already revered Tan; when Tan arrived they sparred head-on in spare, precise language until Sun's thesis collapsed.

sentences.zh: 一坐撫掌大笑，咸稱美之。

translations.literal: The whole assembly clapped and laughed aloud, all praising him.
translations.idiomatic: The room erupted in applause and laughter; everyone praised him.

sentences.zh: 累遷丹陽尹。

translations.literal: He was repeatedly promoted to governor of Danyang.
translations.idiomatic: He rose by stages to governor of Danyang.

sentences.zh: 為政清整，門無雜賓。

translations.literal: His administration was clear and orderly; no improper visitors crossed his gate.
translations.idiomatic: His rule was crisp and disciplined; no stray callers cluttered his door.

sentences.zh: 時百姓頗有訟官長者，諸郡往往有相舉正，惔歎曰：「夫居下訕上，此弊道也。

translations.literal: At the time common people often sued their magistrates; many commanderies had mutual accusations. Tan sighed: 'For those below to mock those above is a corrupt way.'
translations.idiomatic: Commoners were suing their magistrates, and neighbouring prefectures egged one another on. Tan sighed, 'Subjects ridiculing superiors rots the order below.'

sentences.zh: 古之善政，司契而已，豈不以其敦本正源，鎮靜流末乎！

translations.literal: In antiquity good government was nothing but holding the tally—was it not because they strengthened the root and corrected the source, thereby quieting what flowed below?
translations.idiomatic: The ancients governed by holding the tally—because they steadied the root, the branches stayed calm.

sentences.zh: 君雖不君，下安可以失禮。

translations.literal: Though the lord may fail as lord, how may those below abandon propriety?
translations.idiomatic: Even when the ruler misrules, how may inferiors cast off ritual?

sentences.zh: 若此風不革，百姓將往而不反。

translations.literal: If this wind is not reformed, the people will go forth and not return.
translations.idiomatic: Unless this habit ends, the people will drift away and never come back.

sentences.zh: 」遂寢而不問。

translations.literal: He therefore let the matter drop and made no inquiry.
translations.idiomatic: He shelved the suits and investigated nothing.

sentences.zh: 性簡貴，與王羲之雅相友善。

translations.literal: By nature he was concise and refined; he was on excellent terms with Wang Xizhi.
translations.idiomatic: Reserved and fastidious by temperament, he was intimate with Wang Xizhi.

sentences.zh: 郗愔有傖奴善知文章，羲之愛之，每稱奴於惔。

translations.literal: Xi Yin had a rustic slave who understood literary composition; Xizhi prized him and often praised the slave to Tan.
translations.idiomatic: Xi Yin kept a rough-hewn slave who could write; Xizhi adored him and kept praising the man to Tan.

sentences.zh: 惔曰：「何如方回邪？

translations.literal: Tan said: 'How does he compare to Fanghui?'
translations.idiomatic: Tan asked, 'How does he measure against Fanghui?'

sentences.zh: 」羲之曰：「小人耳，何比郗公！

translations.literal: Xizhi said: 'A petty man—how could he compare to Lord Xi!'
translations.idiomatic: Xizhi replied, 'A menial—how could he rank with Lord Xi?'

sentences.zh: 」惔曰：「若不如方回，故常奴耳。

translations.literal: Tan said: 'If he does not match Fanghui, he is after all only a slave.'
translations.idiomatic: Tan said, 'Then he remains a slave—nothing more.'

sentences.zh: 」桓溫嘗問惔：「會稽王談更進邪？

translations.literal: Huan Wen once asked Tan: 'Has the Prince of Kuaiji's discourse advanced further?'
translations.idiomatic: Huan Wen once asked whether the Prince of Kuaiji's talks had deepened.

sentences.zh: 」惔曰：「極進，然故第二流耳。

translations.literal: Tan said: 'It has advanced greatly—yet still only second rank.'
translations.idiomatic: Tan answered, 'Greatly—but still second tier.'

sentences.zh: 」溫曰：「第一復誰？

translations.literal: Wen said: 'Who then is first?'
translations.idiomatic: Wen pressed, 'Who counts as first?'

sentences.zh: 」惔曰：「故在我輩。

translations.literal: Tan said: 'Still ourselves.'
translations.idiomatic: Tan said, 'Still our own circle.'

sentences.zh: 」其高自標置如此。

translations.literal: Thus loftily did he rate himself.
translations.idiomatic: Such was the height at which he ranked himself.

sentences.zh: 惔每奇溫才，而知其有不臣之跡。

translations.literal: Tan always marveled at Wen's ability yet knew he harbored signs of disloyalty.
translations.idiomatic: Tan admired Huan Wen's gifts yet saw the makings of treason in him.

sentences.zh: 及溫為荊州，惔言於帝曰：「溫不可使居形勝地，其位號常宜抑之。

translations.literal: When Wen became inspector of Jingzhou, Tan said to the emperor: 'Wen must not be allowed to hold commanding terrain; his titles and ranks should always be held in check.'
translations.idiomatic: When Wen took Jingzhou, Tan warned the emperor, 'Never leave him astride strategic ground—keep his titles and rank under constant restraint.'

sentences.zh: 」勸帝自鎮上流，而己為軍司，帝不納。

translations.literal: He urged the emperor to command the upper Yangzi himself while he served as army director—the emperor did not accept.
translations.idiomatic: He urged the emperor to command the upper river himself while Tan served as army chief of staff; the emperor refused.

sentences.zh: 又請自行，復不聽。

translations.literal: He again asked to go himself; again he was not permitted.
translations.idiomatic: He volunteered to go himself; again permission was denied.

sentences.zh: 及溫伐蜀，時咸謂未易可制，惟惔以為必克。

translations.literal: When Wen campaigned against Shu, everyone said Shu would not be easy to subdue; only Tan believed he would surely conquer.
translations.idiomatic: When Wen marched on Shu, the court assumed it near impossible; Tan alone insisted Wen would win.

sentences.zh: 或問其故，云：「以蒱博驗之，其不必得，則不為也。

translations.literal: When someone asked why, he said: 'One may test it by dice and board games—if he were not sure of winning, he would not act.'
translations.idiomatic: Asked why, he said, 'Watch him at dice and board—he never gambles unless the odds favor him.'

sentences.zh: 恐溫終專制朝廷。

translations.literal: He feared Wen would end by dominating the court.
translations.idiomatic: He feared Wen would end by bending the capital to his will.

sentences.zh: 」及後竟如其言。

translations.literal: Later events proved exactly as he said.
translations.idiomatic: Later history bore him out.

sentences.zh: 嘗薦吳郡張憑，憑卒為美士，眾以此服其知人。

translations.literal: He once recommended Zhang Ping of Wu commandery; Ping indeed became an admirable gentleman, and on this account people admired his judgment of men.
translations.idiomatic: He nominated Zhang Ping of Wu commandery; Ping proved an outstanding gentleman, and observers praised Tan's eye for men.

sentences.zh: 尤好《老莊》，任自然趣。

translations.literal: He especially loved the Laozi and Zhuangzi and followed natural inclination.
translations.idiomatic: He cherished the Laozi and Zhuangzi and lived by spontaneous inclination.

sentences.zh: 疾篤，百姓欲為之祈禱，家人又請祭神，惔曰：「丘之禱久矣。

translations.literal: When gravely ill, the common people wished to pray for him; his family also asked to sacrifice to the gods. Tan said: 'Qiu's praying has long been done.'
translations.idiomatic: When death neared, locals wished to pray for him and his kin wished to sacrifice; Tan quoted Confucius—'Qiu has prayed long enough.'

sentences.zh: 」年三十六，卒官。

translations.literal: At thirty-six he died in office.
translations.idiomatic: He died in office at thirty-six.

sentences.zh: 孫綽為之誄云：「居官無官官之事，處事無事事之心。

translations.literal: Sun Chuo composed his elegy: 'In office he did no business of office; in affairs he harbored no mind for affairs.'
translations.idiomatic: Sun Chuo's elegy said, 'He held office yet seemed beyond office; he faced affairs yet kept no grasping mind.'

sentences.zh: 」時人以為名言。

translations.literal: People of the time took it as a memorable saying.
translations.idiomatic: His contemporaries pronounced it a perfect epitaph.

sentences.zh: 後綽嘗詣褚裒，言及惔，流涕曰：「可謂人之云亡，邦國殄瘁。

translations.literal: Later Chuo visited Chu Pou and spoke of Tan, weeping: 'One may say: when such men pass away, the state is laid waste.'
translations.idiomatic: Later Chuo visited Chu Pou, spoke of Tan, and wept, 'When men like this vanish, the realm withers.'

sentences.zh: 」裒大怒曰：「真長生平何嘗相比數，而卿今日作此面向人邪！

translations.literal: Pou angrily said: 'In all his life Zhenchang never ranked you with him—why do you put on this face for people today!'
translations.idiomatic: Pou flared, 'Zhenchang never counted you among his peers—why parade such grief before others?'

sentences.zh: 」其為名流所敬重如此。

translations.literal: Thus was he revered by the famous men of the age.
translations.idiomatic: Such was the esteem the leading gentlemen paid him.

sentences.zh: 張憑

translations.literal: Zhang Ping.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Ping

sentences.zh: 張憑，字長宗。

translations.literal: Zhang Ping, style name Changzong.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Ping, courtesy name Changzong.

sentences.zh: 祖鎮，蒼梧太守。

translations.literal: His grandfather Zhen was governor of Cangwu.
translations.idiomatic: His grandfather Zhang Zhen governed Cangwu.

sentences.zh: 憑年數歲。

translations.literal: Ping was only a few years old.
translations.idiomatic: Ping was still a small child.

sentences.zh: 鎮謂其父曰：「我不如汝有佳兒。

translations.literal: Zhen said to his father: 'I am not your equal in having a fine son.'
translations.idiomatic: Zhen told Ping's father, 'You surpass me in bearing a worthy son.'

sentences.zh: 」憑曰：「阿翁豈宜以子戲父邪！

translations.literal: Ping said: 'Grandfather, ought you use a son to make sport of a father!'
translations.idiomatic: Ping shot back, 'Grandfather should not mock father through the son.'

sentences.zh: 」及長，有志氣，為鄉閭所稱。

translations.literal: When grown he had ambition and spirit and was praised in his village.
translations.idiomatic: Grown, he showed drive and was praised in his district.

sentences.zh: 舉孝廉，負其才，自謂必參時彥。

translations.literal: Recommended as filial and incorrupt, he trusted in his talent and believed he would surely join the luminaries of the age.
translations.idiomatic: Recommended filial and incorrupt, he trusted his abilities and expected to walk among the age's leading talents.

sentences.zh: 初，欲詣惔，鄉里及同舉者共笑之。

translations.literal: At first, when he wished to visit Tan, his fellow villagers and those recommended with him all laughed at him.
translations.idiomatic: When he first meant to call on Liu Tan, neighbors and fellow nominees laughed him down.

sentences.zh: 既至，惔處之下坐，神意不接，憑欲自發而無端。

translations.literal: When he arrived, Tan seated him below and showed no warmth; Ping wished to speak up but had no opening.
translations.idiomatic: Tan placed him on a low seat and barely acknowledged him; Zhang burned to speak yet found no opening.

sentences.zh: 會王就濛惔清言，有所不通，憑於末坐判之，言旨深遠，足暢彼我之懷，一坐皆驚。

translations.literal: When Wang arrived to engage Meng and Tan in pure talk and hit a passage he could not follow, Ping from the lowest seat adjudicated it—his meaning profound and far-reaching, fully expressing both sides' intent—and the whole assembly was astonished.
translations.idiomatic: When Wang Meng joined Liu Tan in pure conversation and stumbled over a point, Zhang Ping from the lowliest seat untangled it—his insight so deep it illuminated both sides—and the room gasped.

sentences.zh: 惔延之上坐，清言彌日，留宿至旦遣之。

translations.literal: Tan invited him to the upper seat; they talked all day; he was lodged overnight and sent off at dawn.
translations.idiomatic: Tan moved him to the place of honor; they talked until nightfall and Tan lodged him, sending him off at dawn.

sentences.zh: 憑既還船，須臾，惔遣傳教覓張孝廉船，便召與同載，遂言之于簡文帝。

translations.literal: Ping had just returned to his boat when presently Tan sent a messenger to find the boat of Filial and Incorrupt Zhang and had him summoned to ride together; he then spoke of him to Emperor Jianwen.
translations.idiomatic: Hardly back aboard his boat, Tan sent runners to find Filial-and-Incorrupt Zhang's vessel, pulled him into a shared carriage, and commended him to Emperor Jianwen.

sentences.zh: 帝召與語，歎曰：「張憑勃窣為理窟。

translations.literal: The emperor summoned him and conversed, sighing: 'Zhang Ping stammers yet is a treasury of principle.'
translations.idiomatic: The emperor received him and sighed, 'Zhang Ping seems awkward as a rustic, yet he houses every subtle doctrine.'

sentences.zh: 」官至吏部郎、御史中丞。

translations.literal: His offices rose to director in the ministry of personnel and imperial censor.
translations.idiomatic: He rose to director of personnel selection and imperial censor-in-chief.

sentences.zh: 韓伯

translations.literal: Han Bo.
translations.idiomatic: Han Bo

sentences.zh: 韓伯，字康伯，潁川長社人也。

translations.literal: Han Bo, style name Kangbo, was a native of Changshe in Yingchuan.
translations.idiomatic: Han Bo, courtesy name Kangbo, hailed from Changshe in Yingchuan.

sentences.zh: 母殷氏，高明有行。

translations.literal: His mother Lady Yin was discerning and principled.
translations.idiomatic: His mother Lady Yin was acute and virtuous.

sentences.zh: 家貧窶，伯年數歲，至大寒，母方為作襦，令伯捉熨斗，而謂之曰：「且著襦，尋當作復褌。

translations.literal: The family was poor; Bo was only a few years old. In deep winter his mother was making him a lined jacket and had Bo hold the iron; she said to him: 'Put on the jacket for now; soon I shall make lined trousers too.'
translations.idiomatic: They were destitute; Bo was still tiny. One bitter winter his mother sewed him a lined jacket while he steadied the iron; she said, 'Wear this first—I will stitch lined trousers next.'

sentences.zh: 」伯曰：「不復須。

translations.literal: Bo said: 'We shall not need them.'
translations.idiomatic: Bo answered, 'There will be no need.'

sentences.zh: 」母問其故，對曰：「火在鬥中，而柄尚熱，今既著襦，下亦當暖。

translations.literal: His mother asked the reason, and he replied: 'The fire is inside the ladle, yet the handle is still hot; now that I wear the jacket, below should also grow warm.'
translations.idiomatic: She asked why. He said the coals heat the bowl of the iron yet the handle already burns; with the jacket warming his chest, his legs would soon follow.

sentences.zh: 」母甚異之。

translations.literal: His mother marveled greatly at him.
translations.idiomatic: His mother marveled at the boy.

sentences.zh: 及長，清和有思理，留心文藝。

translations.literal: When grown, he was clear, harmonious, and thoughtful in principle; he devoted attention to letters and belles-lettres.
translations.idiomatic: As an adult he was serene, thoughtful, and devoted to literature and arts.

sentences.zh: 舅殷浩稱之曰：「康伯能自標置，居然是出群之器。

translations.literal: His maternal uncle Yin Hao praised him: 'Kangbo knows how to set his own measure—truly he is talent that stands beyond the crowd.'
translations.idiomatic: His uncle Yin Hao said, 'Kangbo sets his own standard—he is clearly no ordinary talent.'

sentences.zh: 」潁川庾龢名重一時，少所推服，常稱伯及王坦之曰：「思理倫和，我敬韓康伯；

translations.literal: Yingchuan's Yu He enjoyed the foremost renown of the age and seldom deferentially endorsed anyone; he regularly praised Bo and Wang Tanzhi, saying: 'In coherent principle and harmonious human relations I honor Han Kangbo;
translations.idiomatic: Yu He of Yingchuan towered over his generation and rarely praised others; he often ranked Han Bo beside Wang Tanzhi: 'For lucid reasoning and balanced relation I defer to Han Kangbo;

sentences.zh: 志力強正，吾愧王文度。

translations.literal: In resolve and strength of rectitude I fall short before Wang Wendu.'
translations.idiomatic: for force of purpose and firm integrity I bow to Wang Wendu.'

sentences.zh: 自此以還，吾皆百之矣。」

translations.literal: From these two downward, I rate myself at one against a hundred of them.'
translations.idiomatic: Beside those two I count myself at one to their hundred.'

sentences.zh: 舉秀才，征佐著作郎，並不就。

translations.literal: Recommended as cultivated talent and summoned as assistant palace editor—he accepted neither.
translations.idiomatic: They nominated him as a cultivated talent and summoned him as assistant editor of the palace library; he took neither post.

sentences.zh: 簡文帝居籓，引為談客，自司徒左西屬轉撫軍掾、中書郎、散騎常侍、豫章太守，入為侍中。

translations.literal: When Emperor Jianwen held a princely fief he brought him in as a discourse guest; from aide on the minister of education's left western staff he turned to staff officer to the general who comforts the army, palace secretary, attendant gentleman at scattered cavalry, governor of Yuzhang, and entered court as palace attendant.
translations.idiomatic: While Emperor Jianwen still held his princely domain, he kept Han Bo as a salon guest. Han Bo moved from aide under the minister of education to secretary on the heir's staff, palace secretary, attendant at scattered cavalry, governor of Yuzhang, and finally palace attendant at court.

sentences.zh: 陳郡周勰為謝安主簿，居喪廢禮，崇尚莊老，脫落名教。

translations.literal: Zhou Xie of Chen commandery served Xie An as chief clerk; while mourning he abandoned ritual, exalted Zhuangzi and Laozi, and cast off Confucian norms.
translations.idiomatic: Zhou Xie of Chen served Xie An as chief clerk; in mourning he cast off ritual, exalted Zhuangzi and Laozi, and shrugged off orthodox teaching.

sentences.zh: 伯領中正，不通勰，議曰：「拜下之敬，猶違眾從禮。

translations.literal: Bo headed the local appraisal office and denied Zhou certification; he argued: 'The reverence of bowing low—still one must defy the crowd to follow ritual.'
translations.idiomatic: As regional appraiser Han Bo refused to certify Zhou; he argued that bowing in reverence means defying fashion to honor rite.

sentences.zh: 情理之極，不宜以多比為通。

translations.literal: At the utmost of human feeling and principle, one should not take indulgent comparison as permissiveness.
translations.idiomatic: When feeling and principle reach their limit, broad indulgence cannot pass for sound judgment.

sentences.zh: 」時人憚焉。

translations.literal: People of the time stood in awe of this.
translations.idiomatic: His contemporaries respected—and feared—him for it.

sentences.zh: 」識者謂伯可謂澄世所不能澄，而裁世所不能裁者矣，與夫容己順眾者，豈得同時而共稱哉！

translations.literal: Those with judgment said Bo could clarify what the age could not clarify and judge what the age could not judge—how could he be named alongside those who indulge themselves and truck with the crowd!
translations.idiomatic: Thoughtful observers said Han Bo clarified what the age could not clarify and cut through what the age could not settle—how line him up with men who smooth their own way and follow the mob?

sentences.zh: 王坦之又嘗著《公謙論》，袁宏作論以難之。

translations.literal: Wang Tanzhi also once composed On Public Modesty; Yuan Hong wrote an essay to challenge it.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Tanzhi had written On Public Modesty; Yuan Hong answered with a counter-essay.

sentences.zh: 伯覽而美其辭旨，以為是非既辯，誰與正之，遂作《辯謙》以折中曰：

translations.literal: Bo read it and admired its phrasing; holding that right and wrong having been argued, who would set them aright, he therefore composed Disputing Modesty to strike the mean, saying:
translations.idiomatic: Han Bo admired Yuan's rhetoric but, once both sides had argued, saw no arbiter—so he wrote Disputing Modesty to mediate. He began:

sentences.zh: 夫尋理辯疑，必先定其名分所存。

translations.literal: In pursuing principle and debating doubt, one must first fix where names and duties rest.
translations.idiomatic: To trace a doctrine and settle doubt you must first settle where titles and duties lie.

sentences.zh: 所存既明，則彼我之趣可得而詳也。

translations.literal: Once what rests is clear, the tendencies of other and self can be grasped in detail.
translations.idiomatic: Once those are fixed, you can spell out what self and other each intend.

sentences.zh: 夫謙之為義，存乎降己者也。

translations.literal: As for the meaning of modesty, it lies in lowering oneself.
translations.idiomatic: Modesty means lowering yourself.

sentences.zh: 以高從卑，以賢同鄙，故謙名生焉。

translations.literal: Using height to follow baseness, using worth to align with meanness—hence the name modesty arises.
translations.idiomatic: The lofty stoops to the low, the worthy meets the mean—hence the word modesty.

sentences.zh: 孤寡不穀，人之所惡，而侯王以自稱，降其貴者也。

translations.literal: 'Orphan,' 'solitary,' 'unworthy'—what people loathe—yet marquises and kings use them of themselves: lowering their nobility.
translations.idiomatic: Rulers call themselves orphan, solitary, unworthy—terms commoners hate—to humble their own rank.

sentences.zh: 執禦執射，眾之所賤，而君子以自目，降其賢才也。

translations.literal: Charioteering and archery—what the multitude despises—yet the gentleman applies them to himself as titles: lowering his worthy talent.
translations.idiomatic: Charlotry and archery are low trades, yet the gentleman claims them as his roles—another way to mute his gifts.

sentences.zh: 與夫山在地中之象，其致豈殊哉！

translations.literal: Compared with the image of a mountain within the earth—is the import any different!
translations.idiomatic: It is the same spirit as the hexagram image of a mountain inside the earth.

sentences.zh: 舍此二者，而更求其義，雖南轅求冥，終莫近也。

translations.literal: Apart from these two, to seek its meaning further—though you drive the chariot south seeking darkness, you will never draw near.
translations.idiomatic: Beyond these images, groping for modesty's sense is like driving south to find night—you never arrive.

sentences.zh: 夫有所貴，故有降焉；

translations.literal: Because there is something honored, there is lowering.
translations.idiomatic: Honor implies the gesture of lowering.

sentences.zh: 夫有所美，故有謙焉。

translations.literal: Because there is something prized, there is modesty.
translations.idiomatic: Excellence invites the language of modesty.

sentences.zh: 譬影響之與形聲，相與而立。

translations.literal: They are like shadow and echo to form and sound—rising together.
translations.idiomatic: They pair like shadow to form, echo to voice.

sentences.zh: 道足者，忘貴賤而一賢愚；

translations.literal: Those whose way is complete forget noble and base and unify worthy and foolish.
translations.idiomatic: Those complete in the Way forget rank and treat sage and fool alike.

sentences.zh: 體公者，乘理當而均彼我。

translations.literal: Those who embody impartiality ride what is right and fair and balance self with other.
translations.idiomatic: Those who embody fairness ride what is fitting and weigh self against others evenly.

sentences.zh: 降挹之義，于何而生！

translations.literal: Where would the meaning of lowering and yielding arise!
translations.idiomatic: Then where does lowering oneself still matter?

sentences.zh: 則謙之為美，固不可以語至足之道，涉乎大方之家矣。

translations.literal: Then as for modesty as excellence, it surely cannot be spoken of in terms of the utmost sufficiency of the way or applied to the house of the great paradigm.
translations.idiomatic: Thus modesty's praise cannot describe someone already full of the Way or admitted to the greatest teaching.

sentences.zh: 然君子之行己，必尚於至當，而必造乎匿善。

translations.literal: Yet in conducting himself the gentleman must aim at utmost fitness and must arrive at concealing his goodness.
translations.idiomatic: Still, the gentleman pursues perfect fitness and learns to hide his goodness.

sentences.zh: 至理在乎無私，而動之於降己者何？

translations.literal: The utmost principle lies in selflessness—why then act through lowering oneself?
translations.idiomatic: The highest pattern is selfless—why rehearse self-effacement?

sentences.zh: 誠由未能一觀於能鄙，則貴賤之情立；

translations.literal: Truly because one has not yet unified one's view of capability and meanness, feelings of noble and base stand;
translations.idiomatic: Because talent and mediocrity still look different to us, pride and shame persist;

sentences.zh: 非忘懷於彼我，則私己之累存。

translations.literal: If one has not forgotten other and self, the burden of private self remains.
translations.idiomatic: until other and self dissolve, private craving dogs us.

sentences.zh: 當其所貴在我則矜，值其所賢能之則伐。

translations.literal: When what they honor is in themselves they become arrogant; when what they count worthy matches their ability they boast.
translations.idiomatic: We preen when we prize ourselves; we boast when we fancy our powers.

sentences.zh: 處貴非矜，而矜己者常有其貴；

translations.literal: Dwelling in nobility is not arrogance—yet those arrogant toward themselves always cling to their nobility.
translations.idiomatic: High rank need not breed arrogance, yet the vain cling to rank.

sentences.zh: 言善非伐，而伐善者驟稱其能。

translations.literal: Speaking of goodness is not boasting—yet those who boast of goodness suddenly trumpet their ability.
translations.idiomatic: Speaking of virtue need not be bragging, yet braggarts parade every gift.

sentences.zh: 是以知矜貴之傷德者，故宅心於卑素；

translations.literal: Hence knowing that clinging to nobility harms virtue, they lodge the mind in humility and plainness;
translations.idiomatic: Knowing pride in station corrupts character, they settle the mind in lowliness and plain cloth;

sentences.zh: 悟驟稱之虧理者，故情存於不言。

translations.literal: Awakened that sudden self-praise betrays principle, they keep feeling in not speaking.
translations.idiomatic: knowing loud self-praise breaks truth, they guard meaning in silence.

sentences.zh: 情存於不言，則善斯匿矣；

translations.literal: When feeling rests in not speaking, goodness is thereby hidden;
translations.idiomatic: Silence hides the good;

sentences.zh: 宅心於卑素，則貴斯降矣。

translations.literal: When the mind lodges in humility and plainness, nobility is thereby lowered.
translations.idiomatic: humility lowers the show of nobility.

sentences.zh: 夫所況君子之流，苟理有未盡，情有未夷，存我之理未冥於內，豈不同心於降挹洗之所滯哉！

translations.literal: As for gentlemen so compared—if principle is not fully realized, feeling not yet smoothed, the principle of self still not extinguished within—how could they not alike center their hearts on lowering, yielding, and washing away what sticks!
translations.idiomatic: So long as doctrine stays unfinished and feeling unsettled—so long as 'I' lingers within—the gentleman still trains on humility, yielding, and rinsing away attachment.

sentences.zh: 體有而擬無者，聖人之德；

translations.literal: Embodying possession yet modeling emptiness—this is the sage's virtue;
translations.idiomatic: To seem empty while holding fullness is the sage's virtue;

sentences.zh: 有累而存理者，君子之情。

translations.literal: Bearing burden yet preserving principle—this is the gentleman's disposition.
translations.idiomatic: to bear burden yet keep principle is the gentleman's temper.

sentences.zh: 雖所滯不同，其於遣情之累緣有弊而用，降己之道由私我而存，一也。

translations.literal: Although what sticks differs, in casting off the burden of feeling they rely on what is flawed yet useful; in the way of lowering oneself private self still subsists—the principle is one.
translations.idiomatic: Their knots differ, yet both use imperfect tools to shed passion's weight; both paths humble the self because private mind remains—the logic is the same.

sentences.zh: 故懲忿窒欲，著於《損》象；

translations.literal: Hence restraining wrath and stopping desire appears in the image of Diminishing;
translations.idiomatic: Thus curbing wrath and desire belongs to the symbol of Diminishing;

sentences.zh: 卑以自牧，實系《謙》爻。

translations.literal: Baseness to shepherd oneself truly attaches to the lines of Modesty.
translations.idiomatic: grounding yourself to be governed belongs to the lines of Modesty.

sentences.zh: 皆所以存其所不足，拂其所有餘者也。

translations.literal: Both are means to keep what is insufficient and brush away what is excessive.
translations.idiomatic: Both shore up what you lack and scrape away what you hoard.

sentences.zh: 王生之談，以至理無謙，近得之矣。

translations.literal: Master Wang's discourse—holding that at the utmost principle there is no modesty—comes near the mark.
translations.idiomatic: Master Wang's claim that perfect principle leaves no room for modesty nearly hits truth.

sentences.zh: -{云}-人有爭心，善不可收，假後物之跡，以逃動者之患，以語聖賢則可，施之於下斯者，豈惟逃患於外。

translations.literal: It says people harbor contentious hearts; goodness cannot be gathered; borrowing traces of outward things to escape the peril of restlessness—to speak thus of sages is acceptable; applied to those below in this way—does it only escape peril without?
translations.idiomatic: The text adds that people nurse rivalry and scatter their goodness; borrowing outward gestures to dodge unsettled impulse may suit discourse about sages, yet applied to ordinary folk it does more than ward trouble outside.

sentences.zh: 亦所以洗心於內也。

translations.literal: It is also what washes the heart within.
translations.idiomatic: It also scrubs the heart within.

sentences.zh: 轉丹陽尹、吏部尚書、領軍將軍。

translations.literal: He turned to governor of Danyang, minister of personnel, and general commanding the guards.
translations.idiomatic: He rotated through governor of Danyang, minister of personnel, and commanding general of the guards.

sentences.zh: 既疾病，占候者云：「不宜此官。

translations.literal: When already ill, diviners said: 'This office does not suit him.'
translations.idiomatic: When illness set in, diviners warned he should not hold that command.

sentences.zh: 」朝廷改授太常，未拜，卒，時年四十九，即贈太常。

translations.literal: The court reassigned him grand master of ceremonies; before he took office he died, aged forty-nine; he was posthumously awarded grand master of ceremonies.
translations.idiomatic: The court switched him to grand master of ceremonies; before he could assume the post he died at forty-nine and was posthumously titled grand master of ceremonies.

sentences.zh: 子璯，官至衡陽太守。

translations.literal: His son Xuan rose to governor of Hengyang.
translations.idiomatic: His son Han Xuan rose to governor of Hengyang.

sentences.zh: 史評

translations.literal: Historian's appraisal.
translations.idiomatic: Historian's appraisal

sentences.zh: 史臣曰：王湛門資臺鉉，地處膏腴，識表鄰機，才惟王佐。

translations.literal: The historians say: Wang Zhan's house ranked among the highest ministers; his land lay in the richest soil; his discernment neighbored craft; his talent was fit for kingly aide.
translations.idiomatic: The historians write: Wang Zhan inherited ministerial pedigree and fertile home ground; his insight touched subtle craft; his gifts matched a king's counselor.

sentences.zh: 葉宣尼之遠契，玩道韋編；

translations.literal: He echoed Confucius's distant affinity, turning the thongs of his leather bindings as he pondered the Way;
translations.idiomatic: He shared Confucius's long kinship with learning, wearing through bamboo strips as he studied the Way;

sentences.zh: 遵伯陽之幽旨，含虛牝穀。

translations.literal: He followed Boyang's subtle meaning, holding emptiness in valley and female.
translations.idiomatic: he pursued Laozi's hidden teaching and sheltered void within valley and dark female.

sentences.zh: 所謂天質不雕，合于大樸者也。

translations.literal: This is what is called heaven-endowed substance un-carved, matching the great simplicity.
translations.idiomatic: They call this native substance uncarved—kin to the Great Uncarved Block.

sentences.zh: 安期英姿挺秀，籍甚一時，朝野挹其風流，人倫推其表燭。

translations.literal: Anqi's heroic bearing stood tall; his fame filled an age; court and countryside drank his manner; human relations held him as their lamp.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Cheng ('Anqi') towered in heroic grace; his name shook the age; court and countryside savored his manner; peers named him their beacon.

sentences.zh: 雖崇勳懋績有闕于旂常，素德清規足傳于汗簡矣。

translations.literal: Although lofty deeds and splendid merit lacked records on the banners, plain virtue and pure exemplar suffice to pass down on bamboo slips.
translations.idiomatic: Grand deeds might miss the battle banners, yet plain virtue and stainless example earn space on the bamboo slips.

sentences.zh: 懷祖鑒局夷遠，沖衿玉粹。

translations.literal: Huai zu had judgment broad and remote; his pure bosom was jade refined.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Shu ('Huai zu') read situations with calm breadth; his breast stayed pure as polished jade.

sentences.zh: 坦之牆宇疑曠，逸操金貞。

translations.literal: Tanzhi's inner chamber seemed vast; his transcendent conduct was metal true.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Tanzhi's scope seemed boundless; his conduct rang clear as metal.

sentences.zh: 騰諷庾之良箋，情嗤語怪；

translations.literal: He sent up satire on Yu's fine memorial; in temper he scoffed at odd speech;
translations.idiomatic: He broadcast satire on a frank memorial from the Yu clan and mocked occult talk with acidic wit;

sentences.zh: 演《廢莊》之宏論，道煥崇儒。

translations.literal: He unfolded the grand thesis of Discarding Zhuangzi; the Way shone in honoring Confucians.
translations.idiomatic: he broadcast Discarding Zhuangzi and let Confucian teaching blaze forth.

sentences.zh: 或寄重文昌，允釐於袞職；

translations.literal: Some were entrusted at the Ministry of Civil Offices, truly ordering the ducal duties;
translations.idiomatic: Some bore the Ministry of Personnel and steadied the minister's burden;

sentences.zh: 或任華綸閣，密勿于王言。

translations.literal: Some served in the splendid edict hall, toiling at royal words.
translations.idiomatic: others drafted rescripts in the splendid archive and polished imperial language.

sentences.zh: 咸能克著徽音，保其榮秩，美矣！

translations.literal: All could manifest fine repute and preserve their honored ranks—how fine!
translations.idiomatic: All left shining reputations and kept honorable stations—admirable men.

sentences.zh: 國寶檢行無聞，坐升彼相，混暗識於心鏡，開險路于情田。

translations.literal: Guobao's conduct went unremarked; by sitting he rose to that chancellorship; he blurred dark insight in the mirror of the mind and opened treacherous paths in the field of feeling.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Guobao showed no merit yet vaulted to chancellor; he smeared his inward mirror and plowed a crooked furrow through passion.

sentences.zh: 于時疆埸多虞，憲章罕備，天子居綴旒之連，人臣微覆餗之憂。

translations.literal: At that time the borders knew many alarms; statutes were seldom whole; the Son of Heaven sat like pendant tassels strung together; ministers lacked even the worry of overturning the stew.
translations.idiomatic: The frontiers were restless, statutes threadbare; the emperor dangled like warning tassels while ministers barely feared spoiling the cauldron.

sentences.zh: 於是竊勢擁權，黷明王之彝典；

translations.literal: Thereupon he stole momentum and clutched power, profaning the bright king's constant norms;
translations.idiomatic: Guobao seized borrowed force and debased the royal pattern;

sentences.zh: 窮奢縱侈，假凶豎之餘威。

translations.literal: To utmost extravagance he gave rein, borrowing leftover awe from a vicious lackey.
translations.idiomatic: he chased luxury on the coattails of a brutal favorite.

sentences.zh: 繡桷雕楹，陵跨於宸極；

translations.literal: Embroidered rafters and carved pillars spanned past the polar throne;
translations.idiomatic: Embroidered beams and carved columns outreached the throne;

sentences.zh: 麗珍冶質，充牣于帷房。

translations.literal: Lovely jewels and smelted beauties filled the bedchamber curtains.
translations.idiomatic: fine gems and polished beauties packed the inner chambers.

sentences.zh: 亦猶犬彘腴肥，不知禍之將及。

translations.literal: Like dogs and swine fattened sleek, unaware calamity approached.
translations.idiomatic: Like hogs fattened for slaughter, he never saw disaster coming.

sentences.zh: 告盡私室，固其宜哉！

translations.literal: To meet his end in a private chamber—naturally fitting!
translations.idiomatic: He died in private rooms—exactly the fate he earned.

sentences.zh: 荀景猷履孝居忠，無慚往烈。

translations.literal: Xun Jingyou practiced filial piety and dwelt in loyalty—unashamed before past exemplars.
translations.idiomatic: Xun Song ('Jingyou') walked filial piety and loyal service—worthy of older heroes.

sentences.zh: 范玄平陳謀獻策，有會時機。

translations.literal: Fan Xuanping laid plans and offered stratagems—well timed to the moment.
translations.idiomatic: Fan Wang ('Xuanping') offered timely counsel when it mattered.

sentences.zh: 崧則思業該通，緝遺經於已紊。

translations.literal: Song's thought embraced every learning and gathered lost classics from disorder.
translations.idiomatic: Xun Song ranged every study and rewove scattered classics.

sentences.zh: 汪則風飆直亮，抗高節於將顛，揚榷而言，俱為雅士。

translations.literal: Wang's gale was straight and bright; he held high integrity on the verge of collapse—speaking in summary, each was a refined gentleman.
translations.idiomatic: Fan Wang blazed straight as wind and lightning, holding integrity as the state tottered—in sum, both were gentlemen of taste.

sentences.zh: 劉韓俊爽，標置軼群，勝氣籠霄，飛談卷霧，並蘭芬菊耀，無絕於終古矣。

translations.literal: Liu and Han were keen and bright, setting themselves above the crowd; conquering spirit veiled the heavens; soaring discourse rolled away the mist—orchid fragrance and chrysanthemum brilliance undying for eternity.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Tan and Han Bo were lucid and bold, loftier than their peers; their spirit veiled the sky, their talk swept away mist—orchid scent and chrysanthemum fire that history will not fade.

sentences.zh: 贊曰：處沖純懿，是稱奇器。

translations.literal: Encomium: Chuchong was pure and good—called a strange vessel.
translations.idiomatic: The encomium says: Chuchong's purity marked him a vessel apart.

sentences.zh: 養素虛庭，同塵下位。

translations.literal: He cultivated plainness in an empty courtyard; he mingled dust in low station.
translations.idiomatic: He nourished simplicity in an empty court and shared the world's dust from humble rank.

sentences.zh: 雅道雖屈，高風不墜。

translations.literal: Though the elegant way was bent, his high wind did not fall.
translations.idiomatic: Though refinement faltered, his lofty tone never fell.

sentences.zh: 猗歟後胤，世傳清德。

translations.literal: Ah, his later heirs—generations handed down pure virtue.
translations.idiomatic: Ah, his descendants—generation on generation of unstained virtue.

sentences.zh: 帝室馳芬，士林揚則。

translations.literal: The imperial house breathed their fragrance; literati raised their norm.
translations.idiomatic: The throne tasted their fragrance; scholars took their measure as model.

sentences.zh: 國寶庸暗，託意驕奢。

translations.literal: Guobao was dull and dim; he lodged his intent in pride and excess.
translations.idiomatic: Guobao was obtuse and nursed ambition through arrogance and waste.

sentences.zh: 既豐其屋，終蔀其家。

translations.literal: Having enriched his house, at last he roofed his house in darkness.
translations.idiomatic: He fattened his roof-beams, then sealed his house in darkness.

sentences.zh: 荀范令望，金聲遠暢。

translations.literal: Xun and Fan enjoyed fair renown; their metal tone rang far.
translations.idiomatic: Xun and Fan wore fair renown; their bronze voices carried far.

sentences.zh: 劉韓秀士，珠談間起。

translations.literal: Liu and Han were noble scholars; pearl-like discourse rose among them.
translations.idiomatic: Liu and Han were peerless scholars; pearl-bright talk rose between them.

sentences.zh: 異術同華，葳蕤青史。

translations.literal: Diverse arts shared splendor; lush and thriving on the green chronicles.
translations.idiomatic: Different gifts shared one brilliance—lush forever on the green chronicles.
